utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody, and especially to you, Mr. McCloskey. Welcome back. I hope we find you well today. We go briefly in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, this witness I would also request a caution for. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the courtroom. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is -- which is -- was given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keserovic, on the request of the Prosecution, I have to caution you and I will read out Rule 90(E) of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence: "The witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." Sir, did you understand what I have read out to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... thank you. Mr. McCloskey is now commencing his examination-in-chief. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Dragomir Keserovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are you retired from the military?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I am not retired from the military. I was removed from the military by the decision of the High Commissioner for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of June, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was the position that the high rep removed you from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I was holding the office of the assistant defence secretary, and I was in charge of security, and, at the same time, I was the chief of the security section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for what army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what reasons were given by the high representatives to remove you? Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The decision states that the function that I was performing, as a chief of service, and that in that function I have not done enough, in order to trace and arrest the -- those who were suspects of having committed war crimes and that this was, in fact, a sign of my non-cooperation with the national court, and with this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We won't be getting into any of that, General. But can you tell us what -- what your rank was when -- when you left that position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I was major general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic? Okay. It's -- problem is solved. Please continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I should say, General, I won't be asking you about any of that, but, of course, the Judges or General Tolimir may. And before we get into your career further, do you recall being interviewed by Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez back in October of 2000 about this case.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you had a chance recently to review the transcript of that audio-taped interview?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall testifying back in June of 2004 as a Defence witness in this Tribunal for Colonel Blagojevic in a similar Srebrenica proceeding?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to review or listen to the audiotape of that testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is there anything significant that you would change in -- either in your interview or in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: During the interview and in my testimony, there was a dilemma that had to do with my engagement in Bratunac. In other words, in the area where the Krivaja operation was being carried out. And the dilemma was in establishing the exact date when I was there, whether that was on the 17th or the 18th of July. There were arguments for either of those days, but after that, after actually checking and reviewing some documents, I believe that it would have been the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We'll go over some of that in more detail. But did I provide you, in the last couple of days, with some additional documents you hadn't seen before and ask you to study those to see if you could sort out which day it was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And is it, in part, based on that review that you've made up your mind when the -- when this actually happened was [sic]?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've got a little binder in front of you that you just opened. Is there anything in there that might help you with that issue?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The binder contains documents that I was provided by you over the last couple of days. There were some -- there is some intercepts in here and they relate to the movement of the Bratunac Brigade commander, Colonel Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we'll get to that in -- in an hour or two, I hope, and go over some of those documents. But I just want to clear up, is there -- is your decision about what date this is based purely on your own analysis and not by any suggestion or pressure or desire on the part of the Prosecution or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is hard to say that as I sit here. There was no pressure of any kind exerted on me. However, I was shown these documents which suggest that it would be logical for that day to have been the 17th. However, as far as I can recall, I'm not absolutely certain. I cannot confirm this based on my own recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. You testified before, I believe, that you had a -- a war notebook that you had consulted before testifying in Blagojevic. Were you able to consult that war notebook recently on this issue?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No. I consulted that notebook and reviewed it before the interview in the year 2000 with Mr. Ruez. And that helped me to establish the time-line on what it was that I did on those days, those ten -- some ten days in July. And since I still had that dilemma, whether it was on the 17th or 18th, after I returned from the Blagojevic testimony, testifying in that case, I went over that notebook again and the chronology of events and the dates that are noted there although there are -- some dates were skipped because there were no developments on those days, so based on that, my stay in Bratunac should have been the 17th, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you still have access to that notebook?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No. At least when I received the summons for this testimony, for this evidence, I tried to find that notebook, but that notebook remained in the office where I never had access or and I never went back to because when the high representative removed me, I was in Greece [realtime transcript read in error "grace"] at the time and I never had a chance to go back to the office and I was never given any of the material that was in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go over your military career. And normally when I have asked you this before, you've started from the present and gone back, so perhaps that is easiest for you. Can you just briefly describe to us your career, starting, I think -- it may be easier for you when you were removed from the high rep, how long had you that job that you described?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. My last duty was chief of security, the security administration, at the Ministry of Defence, which office I held as of September or October 2002, up until the 30th of June, 2004. Prior to that, from approximately February or March 2001, up until September/October, I was the chief of the 1st Corps of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Excuse me. I'm sorry to interrupt. The 1st Corps, can you tell us what that corps was called during the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we heard that you were the -- the chief of that corps. Were you the Chief of Staff or the -- or the commander of that corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I was the Chief of Staff of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Pardon me for interrupting. You can continue.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Before that, between September or October 1999, up until February, approximately, in 2001, I was the chief of the counter-intelligence department in the security administration of the Main Staff of the VRS. A year before that, on the 1st of September, 1998, up until September 1999, I went back to school. I was in the college for national defence within the Yugoslav Army, in Belgrade. From February 1st, 1997 until August 30th, 1998, I held the same position, the chief of the counter-intelligence department of the security administration, which was at the General Staff of the VRS. As of January 30th up until February 1996, and through 31st January, 1997, I underwent training at the General Staff Academy with the Yugoslav Army in Belgrade. From September or in early October 1995, up until the 31st of January, 1996, I was the commander of an armoured brigade of the 1st Krajina Corps of the VRS. From February 1995, up until September 1995, I was the chief of the military police department with the security administration within the sector for security and intelligence of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was your rank while you were in the Main Staff as the chief of the military police department?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I was lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if you could continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a small intervention and I think this will not be a matter of contention. On page 7, line 6, it says -- it reads: "I was in grace," but I believe the witness said: "I was in Greece."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, this is what I heard. Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. That -- that's a good thing to have cleared up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, if you could continue - thank you - what was your job before the chief of the military police section.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: From October 1993 up to February 1995, I was the commander of the military police battalion in the 1st Krajina Corps of the VRS. From the 14th of September, 1992 up to October 1993, I was the commander of the military police battalion in the East Bosnian Corps of the VRS. From June, the 21st of June, 1992 to the 14th of September, 1992, I was the chief of the security department in the armoured brigade of the 1st Krajina Corps of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. General, and I -- I think we can stop there. I'm sure had you a distinguished career in the JNA with the -- and an education. Can you tell us where were you born?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I was born in a place called Piskavice, some 20 kilometres away of Banja Luka in Banja Luka municipality, in Republika Srpska, in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was your rank when the -- in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I am going to be focussing naturally on that -- those -- that period of time when you were the chief of the military police in the sector for intelligence and security of the Main Staff in the security administration. But is it fair to say that you've had a good education and background, both in -- in a classroom sense and in the practical sense on what the job of the security officer is in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: For that army and for those conditions, I was really well educated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I want to show you a document to use as basically a foundation for you to describe a little bit about the basics of the security position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so could we have P01112.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, this is a document that was shown to you by the Defence in the Blagojevic case. It's one of the documents, I'm sure you will agree with me, that I provided you so you could take a look at it to get ready for your testimony. Can you tell us -- we can see that this document is dated 24 October 1994, and from -- no. For the commander, General Mladic. And can you tell us, is this a document that you had a chance to see while you were in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And could we go to the last page in -- in this document. It may be the third page in English and -- yes, you've got it in the B/C/S. And that signature page, I we think can see this "za" which we know is "for." Can you tell us whose signature that is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This should be General Tolimir's signature. As far as I can remember, General Tolimir's signature that I had opportunities to see on some documents. Judging by its appearance, this should be General Tolimir's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We get a translation in English that is a little unclear. Can you tell us, do you believe this is General Tolimir's signature? We don't want to know what it ought to be or whose signature it should be. We want to know if you can tell us whose signature this is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: One cannot be certain about anybody's signature without an expert graphologist's opinion. However, looking at the general characteristics of this signature, I would be inclined to say that this is General Tolimir's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And having had a chance to review this document - if we could go back to the first pages of both - does it, in your view, reflect fundamentally the basic rules associated with security and intel work at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I looked at the document, or better said, I analysed it. What I could say very briefly about it is that this is an instruction that should have enhanced the efficiency of work of security organs. The security organs should have been alerted by this instruction to what the focus of their attention should be, and the commanders should have understood from this document that the tasks of the security organs and their members are complex and that they are not linked exclusively with the work of the command, in terms of general military tasks. But, rather, that there are also tasks that are within the purview of the security organs. In the first paragraph of this document, there's a little discrepancy in terms of the percentages or rather, ratio, which is 80 to 20. According to the regulations that ratio was defined as two-thirds for counter-intelligence, which would correspond to the 80 per cent here, and one-third was for staff security tasks and other tasks in the command and that also includes the administrative staff tasks, police tasks, the cooperation with the courts and so on and so forth. So this is the only discrepancy that exists in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what do you mean by discrepancy? We see 80 per cent for intelligence, counter-intelligence, and 20 per cent for administrative and staff, military police, and criminal-legal. So how is that different than something else you may have known about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: According to what I know, and according to what the rules defined, the ratio should be two-thirds to one-third. So there is a 15 per cent discrepancy, because this ratio should be 66 to 33. That should be the ratio in percentage terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you see anything wrong with Generals Tolimir and Mladic, facing their particular wartime situation, changing that percentages a little bit to 80:20?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to talk about motives. The only motives that I could mention is for the security organs to be alerted to what the focus of their work should be, and that should be counter-intelligence. And, to a lesser extent, all the other tasks. I don't know what the motive was behind defining these motives. It is very difficult -- behind defining those percentages. It is very difficult for me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I wasn't asking you the motive but I was asking if there would be anything wrong with General Mladic and General Tolimir, if they saw fit for good reason, to change the percentages. Would there have been anything wrong with that, militarily, under the rules, under the ethics of the business, as you knew it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about any rules, the Army of Republika Srpska used the rules that they had adopted from the former JNA. The VRS used those rules. There were very rare cases when some new rules were drafted exclusively for the VRS. Some were drafted like, for example, the rules of service and things like that. However, I'm not aware of the fact that rules were changed in the area of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, again, it's a very simple question. Do you find that there is anything wrong or anything improper with Generals Tolimir and Mladic changing the percentage slightly to concentrate more on counter-intelligence and intelligence than the original JNA two-thirds rule?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I understand your question. The instruction or any instruction is a document with a lower force than rules, and rules are lower ranking than laws. For an instruction to explicitly proffer these particular percentages, there should have been a prior change to the rules. They could have done it, but as far as I know, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me just go over just a bit of these and ask you some particular questions. And I probably didn't ask you what your current profession is? Can you just tell us what that is? Your long answers kind of reminded me of it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I hold a doctoral degree in security and I teach at the security and protection school of the University of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And thank you for that. And I -- and we will be relying on your expertise on many of these questions so I appreciate those scholarly responses but sometimes I'll get more particular and I think you'll get the message when I am. But, thank you. Okay, in looking at this first page, we see it's called "instructions," and we see for what. And then it talks in that first paragraph about: "Because of frequent problems, failures, and irregularities in command and control over security and intelligence organs," and it goes on? And then it says: "With the aim of preventing these and similar problems," he is issuing these instructions and then he talks about the 80:20 situation that we've spoken of. And mentioning intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks and the Trial Chamber has heard a quite a bit about that recently so I'm not going to ask you about that. And -- but then we see in the -- also the section related to military police. Can you tell us, under tasks related to military police, what would the security organs in the -- well, let's start in the brigade. The brigade security organs. We won't go down to the battalion of the brigade. But the brigade's security organ and the corps security organs, what are these military police tasks? Or how are they related to the military police, the security organs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: A security organ, or, rather, the officer of the security organ of either a brigade or a corps, in comparison with the military police, is a professional, and he is tasked with the professional control of the military police unit. What does it mean in concrete terms? The security organ is concerned with the staffing policy and materiel and equipment of his military police unit. He is also concerned with the training of all specialities in the military police. He directly controls the military police services. In the military police, there were seven such services, starting with the duty service, and ending with the crime prevention service. And in between, there was the security service, the search service, the patrol service, the escort service, the traffic, military traffic control service, and, finally, the crime prevention service. We can see the most direct link here between the security organ and the military police unit. Some of the tasks the military security organ can pass on to the commander of the military police unit and demand compliance without talking to the commander of the unit first. This is a direct relationship, or, rather, this is what the security organ does with regard to the military police. The second aspect of that relationship, or, rather, the participation of the security organ in one way or another is his work in the unit command as an assistant commander for security, the security organ participates in the decision-making process, in terms of assessing the security situation and proposing to the commander how to use the military police unit in the unit. The commander can accept the proposal, it -- he can partly correct it and then issue the task, or he can reject the proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where would the job of operational secrecy, keeping the operations -- keeping the secrets of operations, you know, confidential and secret from the enemy? Whose -- what role would the security officer play in that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Every activity, every operation, in addition to the basic decision issued by the commander also entails a number of professional enclosures or attachments to that decision. Every officer in their respective sectors drafts such an enclosure. One of those enclosures is also the plan of counter-intelligence protection measures, and it is the security organ who is in charge of drafting that. He is the one who plans measures of counter-intelligence protection for such an activity an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Excuse me, let me just interrupt and -- are you using the term "counter-intelligence" to include operational secrecy? You know, keeping the -- the operation, the nature of the operation secret, you know, from the enemy and the outside world? Are you including that in this counter-intelligence plan?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No. No, not fully. The general plan for measures of an operation protection is the duty of an operative organ, and he is the one who is in charge of secrecy. It is not the security organ who does that. He can only cooperate in preparing such a plan. However, when we talk about counter-intelligence protection, this means that unit has to counter all the intentions by the enemy to launch counter-intelligence activities of their own, in order to learn the details of an operation. At the plan of protection measures is a general plan, it's a public plan and it applies to all the members that unit, and that plan elaborates the -- all the measures that will be put in place to protect information, and it is binding on everybody in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what role does the security officer play in that, in that plan?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: You mean in a general plan for protection measures or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Both. What you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: A general plan for protection measures is something that is drafted by the operative organ in the command. And such a plan prescribes certain general measures that will be put in place, in order to protect the secrecy of data or documents or, for example, the secrecy of the information channels, the protection of the secrecy of the unit's movements, intentions and everything else. This is very general. And all members of the command participate in that and possibly provide their input. This is a general plan that is drafted, and it is binding upon all unit members. When it comes to the plan of measures for counter-intelligence protection, that plan is exclusively channelled towards preventing the counter-intelligence activities by the enemy against the unit and against its activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And would that include, in this -- in the case of 1995, UNPROFOR or NATO?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of course. Well, yes or probably, General? You've got to make a choice. Or I guess you can try to have it both ways, but I need a serious answer on that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The answer will be yes. However, if you are asking me why, I could tell you how those things were governed and how that could be hidden even from the international forces in the territory of the Republika Srpska, how could that have been kept a secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think we need to get into the details of that, nor I do think it's a big problem that your operational details, your military operational details are being kept secret from anyone but yourself. So that's, I don't think, a line I need to go down with you. All right. Now you said -- you listed seven categories that the security officer in the brigade and the corps had direct control and didn't -- I think you said something, didn't have to consult or inform the commander about. Would any of those seven include the escort of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: If we're talking about the escort service, I can say that this applies to all categories of persons who are to be escorted or moved from one place to another place in the zone of the unit's activities, and there are no restrictions to that. So those could have also been prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about the -- well, one of your seven was the escort service, and you've just talked about that. What about the guarding of prisoners of war at temporary sites when they were -- where they were captured, if that was carried out by MPs with the direction or professional supervision of the security organ. Would that be something that would fit under these seven exceptions, or would that something that the security organ would normally consult or inform the commander about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to POWs and guarding them, there's a slight difference there. On the one hand, we have a situation where prisoners of war are guarded immediately upon their surrender when they are guarded and secured by the unit to whom they surrendered or who took them prisoners. However, if we're talking about a task, to secure a certain place, be it a prisoner of war camp that had been set up pursuant to a decision by the commander, then that would fall or could fall under the security service of the military police, to whom the commander issues the tasks. So it is not the security organ alone that takes it upon himself to guard prisoners of war in an area without that task having been ordered to his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's take a well-known example of Srebrenica where we have large numbers, hundreds and hundreds of prisoners that are guarded, in part, by military police with security officers from the brigade and the corps directing them and they're being transported, in part, by military police from one place to the next in vehicles. This kind of large-scale activity of large numbers of prisoners, would this be the kind of thing that a commander would be informed about from his security officer or his -- the commander of the military police unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: All such activities are something that the commander of the military police unit can carry out without receiving a prior order or task. So one must assume that the commander was informed about such activities even before issuing a task to the military police unit. Somebody must reach a decision as to where the prisoners of war will be located or kept. Somebody must make a decision about their transfer from one position to another position, and that person is always the commander. It's not the senior officer of the security organ or the commander of the military police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And, yes, I -- I absolutely agree with you that that kind of thing doesn't happen in a vacuum without the commander's involvement. But what I'm asking you about -- a security officer, especially like in the brigade, that perhaps does not know, in particular, that his commander has been informed at a given time. Would this be the kind of thing that he would inform his commander, if he didn't know if the commander knew already? Large numbers of prisoners, transport of large numbers of prisoners, guarding those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Obligatory. All activities within the zone of the security responsibility of a specific security organ or in the zone of responsibility of the unit that may have influence on the security situation are something that must immediately be told to the commander of the unit. Prisoners of war, their condition, their numbers, that is something that makes, to say the least or sometimes even endangers, the security situation in the zone and security of the unit, and, therefore, the commander must immediately be informed about it as soon as such information is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So if we go back to those seven areas that you described, including escorting of prisoners, where you have said that the security officer doesn't necessarily have to inform the commander, are those -- can those seven be described as your normal daily routine tasks that the commander doesn't have to be bothered with, or why is it that, as you've said, the commander has -- know these security issues, has to know about large numbers of prisoners but yet these seven tasks, they don't need to know about. Can you give us a little bit of clarity on this seven tasks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The escort service, for instance, when it's necessary, and, you're right, it's not something that happens of its own. So when it's necessary to conduct a transfer or an escort, this is not a regular transport. It's military police escorting under arms a group of people using vehicles, or on foot, providing security along the route, and this is one task in regard to which the security organ can issue an assignment to the commander of the military police unit. He can say, "Because of a demonstrated need, you will organise and provide certain number of military policemen to escort ten buses from Kasaba to Bratunac," for instance. That means that he does not need to even address the commander and inform him about organising the escort. He is carrying out this task because there was a demonstrated need for it to be done, in order to achieve the general task that the unit is carrying out. And as for the modes of transfer, decision can be reached by the commander of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you suggesting, for example, on -- and I know you've testified a bit about this, on 13 July, a security officer could order ten buses full of Muslim prisoners to go to Bratunac without telling or making sure the commander of the Bratunac Brigade was informed of that? Ten buses just showing up suddenly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not saying that. Not at all. The security officer was not authorised and could not have determined that ten buses should travel from Kasaba to Bratunac. However, providing that someone, meaning the commander in the zone, has reached the decision that prisoners of war need to be transported from Kasaba to Bratunac and through logistics organ provided means of transport for this detail, and, in addition, tasked either the security officer or directly the military police unit to secure the POWs and escort them, then the security officer will get involved in the escort service and act within that system. He will not do it outside of the system of command, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: If some unexpected development happens, if some prisoners of war appear somewhere where they weren't expected and they need to be transferred or transported to a more safe location, it has to be the commander of the military police unit who reaches the decision, providing he cannot get in touch with his superior officer. The security officer cannot assume any command role instead of the commander, and he is also duty-bound to inform the commander about all of his activities, if maybe that was what you had in mind. There are no activities carried out by the military police unit without the knowledge of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now you have described for us the basic duties of the brigade and the corps security officer, in some sense, as they work with the military police. Can you describe for us the job of the chief of security of the Main Staff in 1995? But before we get into that, can you first tell us, we all know that General Tolimir was the chief of the Intel -- intelligence and security of the Main Staff and that it had an Intel administration and a security administration. In 1995, who was the chief of the security administration?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Frigate Captain or Colonel, I'm not sure, Beara. Ljubisa Beara; he was chief of security administration. And intelligence administration, it was Colonel Petar Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what -- what sections were within the security administration of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I know that there was the first department or counter-intelligence department. Then there was the analysis department. Department for military police. And as an independent segment at the level, it was the counter-intelligence group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. For the period of the summer of 1995, can you tell us who the top people, the chiefs of each of those sections, were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: In summer of 1995, the counter-intelligence section had Lieutenant-Colonel Maric, I think, at the position -- well, not maybe of a chief. I'm not sure. But he was the most senior officer within that section. In the analysis section, in June -- well, maybe no one. But a colonel was there, I'm not sure between which dates he was there. I think his name was Skorupan, who died, and was replaced after a period by Lieutenant-Colonel Cvijanovic, but I cannot tell you with any degree of certainty when was what. As of February 1995, the first officer in the military police department was myself. I was on my own, so I was both the chief and the clerk -- I was on my own. And the chief of the counter-intelligence group was Colonel Pero Jakovljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is Lieutenant-Colonel Maric, the head of the counter-intelligence group, still alive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I do know that soon after the events, maybe even the end of July, he left the VRS, moved to Serbia, and lived and was employed in Novi Sad, but I lost contact with him, so I wouldn't know what happened next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you briefly describe what the counter-intelligence group did.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The counter-intelligence group is, in a way, group specialised in carrying out counter-intelligence activities and counter-intelligence protection of the VRS in general, its operational components, and, most important, facilities and features. It consisted of operatives officers who were in charge of operative activities - in other words, gathering of information, using means at their disposal - then a group of specialist in charge for operative technology, such as audio and video devices, surveillance, cameras, and other devices that comprise operative technology and technics, as well as a group that was in charge for something we call escort. This group would have vehicles and communication means at their disposal, and they would monitor or survey people of intelligence interest when they were in the area of Republika Srpska. So those were three segments: The operational part, the operational technology or technics, and the escort or surveillance group. That was what the counter-intelligence group consisted of. Their job was to protect the army in general and the most important features and elements of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we've heard that there was a counter-intelligence sector at the Main Staff and that there was a counter-intelligence group that was part of the Main Staff that was in Banja Luka. Are you distinguishing the two now, or are you mixing them up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I do distinguish between them. Counter-intelligence department, or section, was making summaries of the counter-intelligence work of all security organs in depth in units. In other words, they would bring together all the work of counter-intelligence activities of the corps, which would, in turn, do that for brigades and so on and so forth. So they were also in charge of counter-intelligence activities in relation to units and institutions of the army, along that line; whereas, the counter-intelligence group was not tied up to any specific unit or feature. It was tasked with monitoring the entire territory of Republika Srpska and dealing with all issues or gathering information related to all issues of interest for the defence in general. For that purpose, it was structured in a specific way. It had territorial division, territorial deployment, and it had specific detachments through which it could cover the entire territory regardless of the units that were present in any segment of the territory, and it was active above units of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm trying to get an idea of how many people were in the counter-intelligence department at Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: At Crna Rijeka, at the time when I'd be going there, I think, in addition to Maric, there was one non-commissioned officer in charge of administrative tasks, and that was it. Most of the activities were carried out by the chief of administration. Colonel Beara was doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So tell us what Beara's job was then. From a practical level. What was -- what did you see him doing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Practically speaking, Beara's job was -- well, he spent most of his time dealing with counter-intelligence activities. All the reports reaching them that had security content would come to his desk, and his task was to review the information and act upon the information. Namely, he would have to provide feedback by giving guide-lines or tasks to security organs. And now I'm talking about sending information down the chain, and, as far as up the chain, he would make a summary and via the sector or the chief of the sector for intelligence and security tasks, he would inform the commander. Mainly according to suggestions by the chief of sector but, in any case, the commander had the duty and the right to be informed about all available information. In addition to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Who was Beara's direct report? Who did he report directly to, first and foremost?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Immediate superior was General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And where were you -- where was your offices during this period of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Military police section and the counter-intelligence group were located in the command of the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka. That's where I had my offices, next to the counter-intelligence group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So we know -- well, from the wartime map that it's quite a distance to go from Crna Rijeka up around the RS over to Banja Luka with -- with the lines and all. So how long a drive was that, to drive from Crna Rijeka - within the Republika Srpska - to get to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: We would use Puch, a four-wheel drive vehicle, that I took from my previous unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But how long a -- give us an idea of how long a distance -- or how long it took you? How long would it normally take someone? Just roughly. I mean, you're talking about the everyday affairs of what's going on in Crna Rijeka with Beara and others, but yet you're in Banja Luka. So how far a drive is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: It would take, in the wartime conditions, quite a long time. Maybe five or six hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in just roughly -- I know this is difficult. In 1995, how often would you go from Banja Luka to Crna Rijeka and actually see how the work was going there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I did not go to Crna Rijeka that often so that I would be well informed about the activities there. I went there when it was either necessary or when I was called. I think that in the period between the transfer of duty and that was after I have reviewed the situation within all the military police units in the VRS so maybe mid-March, or maybe end of March, and the -- and that was the time also when we prepared the report, so I may have visited Crna Rijeka after that two or three times at the most. The rest of the time I was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's break time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We must have our first break this afternoon, and we will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please sit down again. Our apologies for -- forth and back. We had to discuss a procedural matter in your absence related to another matter. Mr. McCloskey is continuing his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, you were just describing in sort of practical, simple terms the various jobs of the various sections at the Main Staff security administration and some of the people and their jobs. But -- and you were just describing the drive, the long drive, from Banja Luka to Crna Rijeka. So before I go any further, can you tell us of these sections -- well, where did -- where was your understanding that Beara worked out of, that Colonel Beara, where did he work out of? What unit, what location.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as the services are concerned, Colonel Beara was the chief of the security administration, which was one of the units of the security and intelligence sector. And he was with the Main Staff of the VRS. As for military police units, if that's what your question related to and us --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... General, hold on. Hold on. I'll try to make my questions clear. All I wanted to know is where did Beara go to work everyday, where was his work location.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: He worked at the 233 hut in Crna Rijeka. That's where he slept. And he also used the premises as his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And how about the counter-intelligence person, Lieutenant-Colonel Maric? Where did he work out of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: At the same office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And how about the analysis section chief, who you thought was Skorupan?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I did not see him a lot, but we all worked out of two offices. They were one across the other. And when I went to Crna Rijeka, I was in the office with Maric and Beara, and there was also an administrative assistant there. We were all in one office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was the name of the administrative assistant?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Her name was Ljiljana Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you, as chief of the military police section, had your main office in Banja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So my question is for the chief of the analysis section, where was his main office? Was it ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: His main office was in Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And the chief of what you've called the counter-intelligence group, I think you said Pero Jakovljevic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So of the two sections, your section, the military police and the intel group were in Banja Luka; and all the rest were in Crna Rijeka. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No, not the analysis group but the counter-intelligence group and my section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, the counter-intelligence group and your section, the military police group, those are the only sections in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Out of the administration -- security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Another point that might have -- I was slightly confused about is when you were talking about counter-intelligence, and it may have been a translation issue where we went from the counter-intelligence section to the counter-intelligence group, but you talked about one counter-intelligence unit that had several operatives that was doing field-work. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The structure of the counter-intelligence group, approximately, was the following. There was the administration, which was in Banja Luka at the headquarters, and it had two detached units, two or three detached units - perhaps three - one was in Herzegovina, in Trebinje. The other one was in Bijeljina, and I believe that there was one such detached group or unit in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And was that the group that had several operatives that did counter-intelligence work in the field, as you described?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you now describe briefly for us this intelligence, counter-intelligence group that's in Banja Luka, and sort of distinguish it, if you will, between the three groups you've just described?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, in Banja Luka, there was the chief of the counter-intelligence group, his deputy when he was in, in fact. There were times when he wasn't there. Then there was also an assistant for technical equipment -- technical equipment or operative equipment. And then there were several operatives who did field-work. And the operative equipment group was there also. They were in charge of the equipment that was used. And there was also the escort group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I -- I think we can figure out what equipment might be in relation to counter-intelligence work. But what's escort? What does that have to -- what does that group do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Not escort. Not monitoring or surveillance in terms of escorting. Rather, that was surveillance. This was undercover monitoring of individuals who were involved in some activities that were considered enemy activities or were about to engage in such activities. So such individuals would be monitored according to a pre-defined plan, and they would be monitored in the areas where they might engage in such activities. That monitoring was undercover. It was covert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you give us a couple of examples of the kind of equipment that the equipment group dealt with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time, it was rather outdated equipment. We had cameras, still cameras, and movie cameras, record -- tape recorders, UHER reel-to-reel tape recorders. There were some tape recorder, pocket tape recorders, Olympus, which were used for covert recording of various conversations and there, as well as some Nagra-type recording devices. So basically we didn't have much. This was just what was inherited, as it were, from the earlier army. This was from the 1980s, the equipment that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to your section. How many people, if any, did you have working with you, or under you, in the military police section?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: It was only me, and I also had a driver at my disposal. He was from the military police battalion of the 1st Corps. He would accompany me, if required, when I went on such trips.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was your direct supervisor or superior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what your job involved in the year 1995? What responsibilities did you have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The military police section was assigned tasks as follows. There was the personnel department and the department for equipment and technology. And then there was also the training department of new recruits. And then we also had to report using the duty office of the military police, or the duty centre, the reporting went from the lowest level units upward, all the way to the battalion, the military police battalion, within the protection regiment which was part of the Main Staff. So these were the tasks that we were involved in mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned the reporting requirements and yet you received reports from the bottom up. And the Trial Chamber is familiar with the military police battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment located in Nova Kasaba. Is that what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That was the military police battalion, the command of which was in Nova Kasaba. It belonged to the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment. And this was a unit that was attached to the Main Staff of the VRS, the Protection Regiment, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who -- you said it started at the bottom. Who did the military police battalion at Nova Kasaba receive military police reports from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: It received reports from the duty service from the military police battalion at corps level. So it received reports from each corps, according to the various services of the military police, and depending on how they were employed on that particular day. The corps would compile reports from the brigades, from the platoons or detachments within -- or companies within the brigades. So, in other words, they would receive their reports from the corps battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So was this a daily reporting requirement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was daily reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So let me make sure I understand this. The brigade military police units reported to their corps, and the corps military police units took those reports -- made their own reports and sent those to Nova Kasaba; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So Nova Kasaba gets reports from all six or seven corps, I -- of military police. And what does the Nova Kasaba -- what do those people do with all those corps reports?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: They would compile a single report where they would sum up the most important points, according to the methods that had been agreed on. So they would pick out -- pick out the most important information from all of those reports and then forward it to the Main Staff as one single report, or, rather, to the security and intelligence department of the Main Staff. In parallel to this, there should be also a report that would go to the commander of the Main Staff, and I'm not sure if that happened every time, and to the commander in charge of security and intelligence. So every day, they would have to be sent to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We got a translation that it should -- that it went to the commander of the Main Staff, and I think we all understand that that was General Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then our translation said that it went to the commander in charge of security and intelligence.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: To the chief of the security and intelligence services sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we all agree that General Tolimir was not a commander at that time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in whose name do you recall that the reports from Nova Kasaba went out from? Who signed off on those -- those big military police reports that came out of the Nova Kasaba MP unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: They should have been signed by the commander of the unit there. But I'm not ruling out the possibility that sometime they were signed by the commander of the unit for the military police services, which united all of those services. And that would happen in the absence of the commander. He was the one who prepared those reports, but it should have been the battalion commander who signed the reports and the reports were dispatched on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in July of 1995, who was the commander of the military police battalion whose name these reports should have gone out under?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The name should have been Zoran Malinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if not Malinic, if he was absent or unavailable, who would be the next person whose name you may see on a report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the family name of a commissioned officer -- a non-commissioned officer who was the commander of the platoon for the military police in the police -- in the military police battalion. I know him -- I remember the face, but I can't put a name to that face. It is possible it was his name that went on the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you've told us generally who these reports went to at the Main Staff, but can you tell us whose desk they actually fell on at the Main Staff in Crna Rijeka? Who would actually see these report -- this -- this report from Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: They should have arrived at General Tolimir's desk. And they should have also landed at the desk of General Mladic, but that was not always feasible. If is possible that they arrived at the operations centre of the Main Staff. And then, from there, they were distributed and sent to General Tolimir and General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was the means of communication of these reports from Nova Kasaba to Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: There was a courier service, there were vehicles, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So hand-delivered by couriers in vehicles.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you get these Nova Kasaba reports in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I did not receive those reports. Only occasionally I would get excerpts, coded excerpts, through the counter-intelligence group when something was really of some importance. But I did not receive those reports on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me ask you about these coded reports. We're familiar with the simple system of teletyping and the code mechanism that was able to encode teletyped communications over radio waves. This coding you just referred to, is that different than that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The system was technically the same. However, the security administration -- or, rather, the sector for security and intelligence, which also means the security and intelligence administration, had a special code that they used with the corps commands, or, rather, the security departments in the corps commands, and that communication went along a parallel line with the line of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell me, was that done by a machine like the one attached to the -- to the teleprinter, or was it oral codes communicated via oral radio lines or telephone lines?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Teleprinters were used. Machines were used. The code itself was different. For example, if a message was coded and sent to a unit, the same teleprinters were used but the code was changed, depending on the sender and the recipient. For example, if they were sent by the security organs, the code was different than the one used by the command. But the equipment was the same. The teleprinters that were used were the same ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we have seen in our collection of Muslim documents that occasionally the electronic decoder attached to a teleprinter didn't work and -- didn't work properly, and documents were sent out in the open by mistake and were actually captured by the opposing side. Were you aware of that possibility?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know of any specific instances. However, it is possible that mistakes happened, like with any other piece of technical equipment. I don't know much about that. In any case, every security department in the corps had or at least should have had a person in the intelligence part who dealt with the electronic equipment and the equipment conveyance of messages which also implied the electronic protection of the unit's communication. Those people were experts in communication and if we are talking about mistakes I don't know what they may have been. I am aware of the instances when a document could not be opened which rendered it worthless. I'm not sure that a message was sent in the open. At least, I've not seen any such messages. I was not aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did the VRS have the capability of sending message -- messages that themselves were encoded? For example, taking a message where, instead of the word, the word was given different numbers to represent the same word. So the message is coded. So even if the other side manages to intercept the message, all they get is gibberish from the code. Did you have the ability to do that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: That was the way we operated. There were two codes. An entry code or the one that was used when messages were sent out, and that code was used for a message to be translated into the code language and sent. On the other side, the end user used a different code that he used to decode the coded message. So an intercepted coded message was not easy to open. That was the idea. Professionals and -- who dealt with those things over a period of time were in a position to perhaps come up with a key, if they had several hours at their disposal to decipher the 30 letters of the alphabet. However, it was a tall order and a strenuous exercise and there was not always enough time to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then -- we're talking about sending written communications that you're coding, as you've said, twice like that. What about oral communications? Just speaking into the telephone. Did you have the ability for someone to speak into the telephone and speak in a code instead of saying, The attack is at dawn, say, 1, 2, 6, 4, 5, 3. Did you have the ability to speak orally in codes like that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were code books. That's what we called documents in which every term was changed, every word was replaced by a letter code or a symbol or a numerical code and that code book was used for all important telephone conversations and in all radio and radio-relay communications. And so on and so forth. In other words, we used code books. People were not allowed to use so-called open communication. And that type of communications did not require the involvement of any technical equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are you aware that if a code book like this is only used once, that, is it possible to break a code from a code book that is only used once, the so-called one-time pad? Even today in today's technology, does that remain a secure means of communicating?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was certainly more secure than the technical modulation of information. It is still used today. The efficiency of such protection is achieved by changing those code tables or code pads. Some were changed daily; some were changed weekly; some were changed monthly. But in any case, those code tables changed, and they were always changed wherever -- whenever there was a suspicion that there was a leak of data or when a code table was compromised. When that happened, another code table was automatically introduced to replace the compromised one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. While we're on this topic of reporting and coded reports, could we go back to the document that should still be on the screen. It is P01112. And if we could go to page 2 in the English. And it's under paragraph 4 in the document, which I think is on page 2 of the B/C/S as well. And it's just that first part of paragraph 4 I want to ask you about, because it talks about reporting of the security organs. It says: "The security and intelligence organs at all levels must submit to ... superior organ in the professional sense, in a timely fashion and ... prescribed form, security and intelligence reports in accordance with the rules of service and the instructions on applying work methods and means of the VRS OB." It talks about keeping the material as a military secret and strictly confidential. In the year 1995, can you -- was there a secure reporting system whereby reports from the security and intel organs of the brigades were reported, the corps reported, and those were sent on to the Main Staff. Or -- could you describe that briefly, as you just did the military police set-up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The military police is a unit which at least at the battalion level had both technical and personnel equipment to comply with the requirements of regularity and the form of reporting. The problem of reporting in this way, as described under bullet point 4, could appear in units such as brigades, which in their areas of responsibility, and on their axis did not have or almost did not have any coding equipment or teleprinters or any other way that they could use in order to convey information. This means that security organs in those units encountered problems. A lot of units, a good part of the units in the army - I don't know how many - were without those pieces of equipment. No problems were encountered at the corps level and at the level of those units which in one way or another were either closer to the corps or those units that had infrastructures that had existed before the war. All those units that were set up during the war faced a lot of problem regarding the communications equipment. So this could be implemented conditionally, and this is how things were envisaged. However, in practice, I don't think that there were conditions in place for full compliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm particularly interested in the Bratunac Brigade, the Zvornik Brigade, and the Milici Brigade. And this Trial Chamber has seen reports, I think, from most all those brigades, the daily combat reports, for example, from the command, being teletyped securely up to the corps. So given those brigade and if they had the -- that we've seen before, the teletyping reporting ability, describe how the brigade security reports start in the brigade, and go upward, if they do.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the same way, which means when somebody wants to send a report, somebody in the security organ, somebody in the brigade, if they want to send a report to the security department in the corps, they had several methods at their disposal. One is to put a document in the mail and address it to the security organ of the corps and a remark, Don't open. The second way is to use the coding equipment, the teleprinter that the brigade had but to use their own code in drafting the document and sending it by means of that technical equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What I'm particularly interested in was there a routine reporting requirement as you described for the military police reports. You said that that was a daily requirement that all the military police had to send daily reports and those went daily to the Main Staff. Was there such a routine daily requirement for the security organs of the brigades to send to the corps that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. The security organs were not duty-bound to send daily reports. They had to keep their superior security organ abreast of developments and they sent out reports as needed when they had information that needed to be sent out. In other words, there were no formal reporting requirements. The security organs, as far as I know, you have to bear in mind that I was not a member of any security organ in the counter-intelligence part during the war, but I know that they did not have an obligation of daily reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And my question was regarding the brigades. How about the corps? Did the corps have an obligation to provide routine reports to the Main Staff, the security branch of the corps -- that is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The corps security department sent out daily reports to the sector of the intelligence and security of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And whose desk would those fall on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: It depended on the method of sending. If they were sent out by communication means, when they were received, they would be packed and then they would be given exclusively to the chief of the security and intelligence services department, or the person who replaced them or stood in for them. In other words, such reports ended up on the desk of the chief of the security and intelligence sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that would be, in 1995, who?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I probably didn't give you a chance to really -- can you just describe your job briefly, as I ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me about my work in the police -- military police department? During the six or seven months that I spent there, the first month was dedicated to tour all the military police units in the VRS. The commanders rallied in one place, in the zone of responsibility of the corps. After that, we issued some documents, some instructions regarding the staffing policy and enhancing the strength of the military police units. My other tasks had to do in some way with the drafting or checking and confirming the training programmes for the members of the military police units, and that primarily concerned the recruit contingent. My other tasks were daily tasks, as part of a process which contained constant issuing of requirements and guiding the work of the military police services. Those tasks concerned gathering reports and feedback which concerned the work of certain units in the military police, as well as certain services in the military police. That is as far as the departments or sections went. However, so far, we haven't said anything about what I also did sometimes. It was my obligation which sometimes lasted for longer periods of time. From the security administration, I was seconded to various temporary bodies and organs or command posts that had been set up by the Main Staff. For example, the forward command post in the western part of Republika Srpska in Drvar, in Mrkonjic Grad, and so on and so forth. There were times during the sudden changes of the situation, especially in the units in the western part, I would be sent out to analyse the situation and to draft reports about the situation I encountered. For example, on the 19th of March, during an offensive launched by the 3rd and 7th Corps of the BH Army against Mount Vlasic, I arrived at the command post of the 1st Corps on Mount Vlasic and I stayed there for nearly a month. The second example would be a situation when I went to the Novi Grad Brigade area of responsibility. And so on and so forth. That means that I often went to the areas where things were happening in order to take stock of the situation and to monitor the developments and report on them. I did that, in addition to all of my other normal everyday tasks. And those things happened very often. Such tasks were given to me quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we'll get, as you know, to a couple of examples of -- of those assignments. And let me go to one right now, which is reflected in a document, 65 ter 7316. I think that may be one that you have the actual physical copy of. It's a bit lengthy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, this is something that was not on our original 65 ter list but something I showed the General in proofing that he was able to be helpful with. And I don't think there will be a problem with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see any objection by the Defence to add it to the 65 ter exhibit list. Leave is granted. Mr. McCloskey, we note that the witness has a binder in front of him. Could you explain what kind of binder of documents is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, General, I think you told us you had some of the documents I gave you. And what else do you have? Can you just tell us what -- what you've got in front of you for the Judges.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: It's just an empty notebook; transcript of interview conducted by Mr. Ruez in year 2000 in Banja Luka; this is the instruction we've seen on the screen, I was given this document by Mr. McCloskey yesterday. We've already seen it on our screens. Then a transcript of intercepts - let me just find them - from the command of the Bratunac Brigade, also given to me by Mr. McCloskey. These are the notes for the witnesses, so it's of no importance. And this is a copy of diary of events kept by the Zvornik Brigade. I also received it yesterday. An excerpt from an order issued by the Main Staff dated 17th of July, 1995, where I'm assigned to carry out certain activities. Those are the documents I have before me. I received them from Mr. McCloskey yesterday, and I brought them along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is a good clarification. All documents you have in front of you, you received from Mr. McCloskey, except the empty notebook; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now this is a bit of a lengthy document, and I don't intend to go through it all. But we can see that it's dated 18th of March, 1995 to the commander of the Main Staff and to the assistant commander for security and intelligence of the Main Staff, and to the commands of the corps. And it is entitled: The analysis of the situation in the military police units in the Army of Republika Srpska. And it's a -- in fact, a lengthy document that goes into the -- analysing the situation of those units. And at the end of it, if we could go to page -- should be 13 in the -- in the English and 7 in the B/C/S? We see it under the name of chief, Colonel Ljubisa Beara, and then we have initials DK/LJS. Have you had a chance to study this document a bit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I believed we -- I believe we looked at a different document yesterday. I cannot remember all the elements of this document. This is an assessment of the situation, whereas, yesterday we looked at a document that had to do with the replenishment and reinforcement which is a shorter document and is a consequence, it's something that arises from this document. So I haven't seen this document before, but DK/LJS means that I did take part in the drafting of the document. It took me almost a month and that it was typed by my assistant Ljiljana Stojanovic. All of this was monitored and finally signed by the chief of administration, Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember the document you saw yesterday that was an original document that we gave you because it was hard to read? And you got an original document.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
