utterances.text: I did see a document yesterday, but not this document that's on the screen right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing the document that had a handwritten section in it that was addressed to Toso?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that. And that was in the document we've seen yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's -- let's go to the first page of this document in both languages. And now let's go to the second page in both languages. So let's keep it in the B/C/S version where we see it says: "Toso" in a handwritten format. Let's go to the next page in the English. Yes, and bring up that Toso part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now it may have gotten a little confusing, General, but the document you see on your screen now is a copy of what we gave to you of the original of yesterday and it's the very document that is on the screen, the one where you drafted the report on the situation of the military police. And you'll recall Mr. Janc was in the room, and I believe he asked you who Toso was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This part in handwriting I have no doubts I have seen that part. But the first page of this document is different than the one we've seen, because the documents we looking at yesterday was called replenishment and reinforcements of military police units; whereas this document, which has the word "assessment" in its title is a broader document, a document that preceded the documents you've shown me yesterday. Although both of the documents as page 2, have this page that's before us now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. General, I'll have our people check and see. I thought there was only one document with this handwritten section emplaced in it. But can you tell us who -- do you recognise the handwriting in this -- this note addressed to General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, this is the handwriting of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I don't think we need to go through all the comments of General Mladic, but just to give us a rough idea, we see from number 1 that he begins by saying: "It is a disgrace to have a soldier commanding a unit after three years." And then at the end of the paragraph he says: "Ensure that every MP unit has an educated and trained officer by 1 July, 1995." And if we go to the next page in the English, we see he goes on making other comments, ensure this, ensure that, including in number 3, he says: "Commanders do not have the right to prevent security organs and military policemen from doing their duties." Then he underlined the -- underline the exclamation point in the B/C/S: "On the contrary, they must assist them to the maximum!!!" And then he goes on, and I won't go over it and I won't go over all your report about the condition of the military police. What I more want to get into it is what this can tell us about the way the Main Staff worked. We see you -- can you tell us -- I think you made reference to this briefly, but did you go anywhere with anyone to get the information that allowed you to draft this report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The section for military police, the military police section, until February 1995 existed only on paper. There were no officers in that section. And then a decision was reached for me to be moved from the military police section or department of the 1st Corps to this section. And the reasons can be seen in the very conditions in the military police units, because the situation in some such units was far below the required level. There were many reasons for such a situation. Very few units had original set-up even before the war. Most of the units that comprised the VRS were set up during the war itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, General, I -- I -- I'm sorry to interrupt you, but that -- the topic you're getting on is the subject of this document, which will go into evidence and it is really too much for us for today. And I think you have testified, as have others that there is under-strength units and difficulties within the VRS in this regard and I don't think that's -- that's an issue. But getting back to my particular question was, in drafting this document, did you go anywhere -- or before drafting this document, did you go anywhere with anyone to allow you to obtain the information to draft this document? Very simple question. Of course, you can always explain it, but we need to get an answer first.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, together with Colonel Beara. I toured all the corps. And in each of the corps, we brought together all level commanders of all military police units, asked them to report about the situation in their units and to provide written reports in addition to the oral report, and all those reports we compiled them together into this report that we see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not you were shown General Mladic's comments to your report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall, but most probably, bearing in mind the fact that this document is dated 18th, and, on the 18th, I was still at Crna Rijeka. I left on the 19th. It is possible I've seen it. I cannot say with any degree of certainty, but there wouldn't have been any reason for me not to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us, just sort of functionally and procedurally, why is it that General Mladic would be addressing the issue of the condition of the military police in the VRS to General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Main Staff is the commander of all troops. Why is he addressing General Tolimir? Well, because General Tolimir was his assistant for security and intelligence affairs, and a part of the professional activities needs to be acted through the sector for security and intelligence and security administration, but that cannot be done in such a way that General Tolimir issues such assignments. Only General Mladic can do that. Only the commander of the Main Staff can issue -- or assign tasks to military police units. In this sense, you cannot have within the chain of command -- you cannot have General Tolimir appearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see that General Mladic is telling General Tolimir, Ensure this happens, ensure that happens. When General Mladic issues that directive to General Tolimir, is General Tolimir duty-bound to see to it that General Mladic's wishes are carried out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: He is duty-bound, except in the cases when the law provides him with an opportunity not to carry out an order, and there were such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of course. If it was an illegal order, for example.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Or carrying out an order that is illegal or a crime in itself. In such cases, any individual could have responded by saying, No, I will not carry out that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In fact, you said any individual that receives such an order could refuse. Is that correct? Aren't soldiers duty-bound that they must --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... which is correct? Could refuse or must refuse an illegal order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Should. Should have refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- better you choose your words as opposed to mine. Fair enough. So in this particular directive, is General Tolimir expected to issue instructions or orders pursuant to what Mladic has told him to do? For example, ensure proper training for the military police.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: What we see here is expectations, and I think that's what we did. It was expected from General Tolimir to prepare, draft a document, that General Mladic would later issue as an order, including the guide-lines that we can see in this list in the document before us. General Mladic is not drafting documents here. Everybody is making sure and, in this case, we're talking about General Tolimir, he was duty-bound to use our assistance, of course, in drafting an order, a document, that would have General Mladic as the signatory and which would then be sent out to units because the units, the subordinate units, know that it's only General Mladic who can issue orders to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've heard quite a bit of evidence that an assistant commander makes a proposal to his commander, gets an order based on that proposal by the commander, and that he is -- the assistant commander is duty-bound to monitor the carrying-out of that order to see to it that it gets carried out properly, because of their expertise they're the ones that should know best whether that order is carried out properly. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we actually saw in the case of Colonel Salapura that he was able to order people to do things pursuant to orders he'd received from his superiors, as long as it was consistent with the orders he received. Is that possible as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know if the sabotage detachment was under directing or control of Colonel Salapura. The relationship was the same and legally, he couldn't have been issuing them assignments. But, in certain conditions, in certain situations where units would recognise Colonel Salapura as an authority for sabotage and reconnaissance tasks. They would maybe accept it. The same things may have happened within the military police but, legally speaking, that is not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: An assistant commander, can they pass on an order of their commander? Not issue it themselves, but if Mladic issues an order saying, I want this hill taken, General Tolimir, pass that order onto Colonel Pandurevic. In that case, can General Tolimir pass on the order to General Pandurevic? Anything wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The rules allow for the commander - specifically, in this case, General Mladic - to tell General Tolimir, You go to the Zvornik Brigade and you will convey my orders to him. And then he tells him the order itself. But that is still an order issued by the commander that was only conveyed by an authorised officer from the Main Staff. So it is possible to do it indirectly. However, as soon as possible, a written order issued by General Mladic and signed by General Mladic should follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mentioned briefly that there were instances of -- I'm not sure you said "illegal orders," but it sounded like that. Did you say that there were instances of illegal orders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that I know of existence of such illegal orders. What I'm saying is that I cannot rule out the possibility that some professional officer organs, for instance, chief of artillery, issues an order to move an artillery group or chief of security to send out a military police unit, things like that were happening, but that does not encroach upon the rights provided by the rules. I'm saying that things may have happened but it's not according to the rules. If they did, it wasn't according to the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. One last short topic before -- before the break, I believe. I should know by now when the break is. You talked about a relationship between Mladic, Tolimir, and Beara in the last trial. Can you tell us what -- what their relationship was, how it was forged in the history of the conflict? It was a very brief historical backdrop of -- relating to General Tolimir and General Mladic and Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And we would appreciate if you could switch off your microphone while receiving the answer and if Ms. Stewart is typing. We always hear this noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I will -- we will make sure that there's no typing during that, but turning it off and on every time, unless I'm making -- if I'm making noise -- well, of course, I will do whatever I'm told. We will try very much not to -- not to make any noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not going to use this document anymore, so I would like to tender 7316.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7316 shall be assigned exhibit number P2216. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what I know is the following. General Tolimir and Colonel Beara were officers of the security administration in the Naval Military District in the former state, and they'd known each other from back then. I think Beara was the chief of security of this Naval Military District, and General Tolimir was member of either one of the sectors or one of the units there. In the meantime, as far as I know, General Tolimir moved to the Knin Corps of the JNA in Croatia, where General Mladic was also serving. He was first Chief of Staff -- or, no, operative officer, then Chief of Staff, then the commander of the corps. I also know that when Colonel Beara was in the blockade in Split, the Knin Corps came to assist them, and from that time, I know that Colonel Beara was always grateful and expressed his gratitude to General Mladic and the 1st Knin Corps. So their relations and the friendship arises from the situation in Split and the attempts to lift the blockade of the Split unit. I could also observe that they had fair relationships. Between General Tolimir and General Mladic, the relationship was more professional, military type, more strict, according to hierarchy. Although they may have been friendly as well, but only at the second level; whereas, Colonel Beara was a kind of officer who would very much act in a less military manner, not strictly according to the rules, so to speak, but I've never noticed that there were any problems because of that. But they were certainly three officers who had been brought together by different situations and conditions and who were doing their best in the position that they were. It may have seemed that they were more friendly than other officers between themselves, but that's about all I can say about their personal relationships.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify something. When the Knin Corps, General Mladic at its head, broke the blockade that was -- that Colonel Beara was caught in, was that during the -- the war years of 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No. That was in 1991. They didn't even manage to get into Split but they achieved the release of the officer. He managed to get very close to Split but not enter it. But all that was in 1991, during the armed conflict in Croatia. That was in no way related to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And that's what I said, so I don't know what translation you got, but I think that's clear. And just one last point before the break that you had mentioned on this same topic when you testified before. You also had mentioned at some point in the career, General -- or Colonel Beara was superior, or Mr. Beara was superior to Mr. Tolimir. And then in the VRS, Tolimir became superior to Beara. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I heard 1992. And, yes, according to my information, Beara was higher in the hierarchy than General Tolimir; whereas, in the VRS, General Tolimir became the chief of service and chief of sector. He joined before General -- or Colonel Beara joined the VRS. Maybe six or seven months before him. Tolimir was already chief when Beara came. Sometimes you could hear Beara mention it within the premises of his office, office of the administration, but it didn't amount to much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's break time. And, Mr. President, I do have an update on the last situation that should resolve the issue, and I can give that to you, of course, at any point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is perhaps better to receive this information before we break. Then, in that case, we should ask the witness to leave the courtroom for the break. And then we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must have our second break and will resume 6.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness should be brought in, please. Mr. McCloskey, would you please indicate the length of the remainder of your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're done with the -- the part about rules basically, and I wasn't really sure how long that was going to take. You could see how he was taking his time, which was fine. Now I have documents related to the events, and it's not as many as Mr. Salapura but I think it's going to be a similar awkward situation, I think, in these discussions. How long that will take, it's got to be within the three hours that's fundamentally left over, and I'm hoping it will be done sooner than that. It really is hard to say. I'm hoping an hour, an hour and a half, two, would be nice, but there's intercepts, there's documents, and it depends on how long his answers are, really, but it is not as much material as the witness before that. But I would hope -- I would hope two hours, maybe the full three more, but I hope not. I would like to -- you know, sit down sooner than later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Though I do have one issue to clear up with him from the last topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for your information. We hope you will be able to finish as soon as possible. Please continue your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. General, I want to go back to that document that you thought we'd given you a different one than you were looking at on the screen. But for our purposes it should be -- P2216 is the one on the screen. But we've gone to the investigator, Dusan Janc, who is the one that gave you the original copy of that document, and he's allowed us to retrieve it. So I want to give you the same one he believes he gave to you. It's the only thing we have, just so we can try to clear that up if we could get some help from the usher --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, with the assistance of the usher, yes, please. Now it was handed over to the witness. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that's what we handed you I think yesterday. Though, as you know, we handed you a few other documents, so you may have got it mixed up or there may be something within that group that you're thinking of. But just take your time, take a look at it, and ... If you could, for just one second look at the screen, you can see the Serbian screen there's that rather distinctive handwritten section in the right-hand corner with the little box around it. Is that the same thing you've got on the original, on that front page of the original?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So any -- can you clarify that for us? Does that look like the one that we showed you yesterday, now that you've had a chance to look at the original?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this is probably the same document. What confused me subsequently was the fact that at one point you called for page 13, or something like that, and now, as I look at it, I do believe that it's the same document. However, it doesn't have as many pages as I was led to believe, 13 or more. So I thought that there were some attachments to the document, but it's quite all right. Yes, I probably got confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, there's 13 pages in the English translation, and it stretches out the document a lot. That's probably the trick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document should be given back to the Prosecution, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's get onto basically June and July of 1995 and some of the events. Can you tell us, General, what your assignment was prior to the attack and fall of the Srebrenica enclave? Basically June, July. Do you remember what you were doing before being sent over to the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Just before I arrived at the Main Staff and was sent to Bratunac, I was in the Novi Grad Brigade of the 1st Krajina Corps with a team from the Main Staff which was tasked with performing an analysis of the causes and reasons for the brigade to lose its positions in the Bihac theatre. So that was my task, some ten days before this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And from the -- from that theatre, were you directed to go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No. From that theatre, I returned on the 16th, together with the team, I returned to the Main Staff in Crna Rijeka, and I went there, bringing with me the information that we had gathered while we were in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what month was that? The 16th of what?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you've already talked about corrections made to your previous testimony about this, whether you went to the Bratunac area on the 17th or 18th. Knowing what you know now, having reviewed the documents, your own material, can -- are you sure that you got back to Crna Rijeka on the 16th, or could it have been on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I think, as far as I know, it was the 16th. It could not have been the 15th. Out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And about what time did you arrive in Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: We arrived in Crna Rijeka sometime during the afternoon. I can't tell you exactly what time it was, but it was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you say "we." Who did you come back with? Who did you arrive to Crna Rijeka with.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the organ, or, rather, the sector for morale and legal affairs, there was Lieutenant-Colonel Dubovina. And there was another officer from the operations administration, the operations organ, whose name I cannot recall, and I could not actually trace back or find any -- anything that would suggest what his name was. And there was the driver, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you report to when you came to Crna Rijeka that afternoon of 16 July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: We went to the command post in Crna Rijeka, the two huts that I mentioned earlier, and when we got there, I can't recall who the first people we got in touch with were, but I know that we were directed to go to an underground command post because the work of the command was actually transferred. It was moved from those huts to the underground command post because of the possibility of some of the forces going, moving from Srebrenica to stumble upon these huts and the command post there, and from there, we went, or at least I did, I can't recall if everyone else went with me, I went to the underground command post and to the operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, because, as far as I can recall, there were no officers there who could be the recipients of the report that we were preparing and who would be able to debrief us on what we -- what it was that we had been engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what happened when you got to the operations room?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, we did our part of the job there. I can't recall every detail, but we handed over whatever material we had gathered on our previous mission. And sometime in the evening, about 6.00 or 7.00, or, rather, 1800 or 1900 hours, the commander of the Main Staff entered the operations room, and he told me right away that I was more than welcome and that he had a mission for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so this was General Mladic, I take it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you receive any information where he had come from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did General Mladic tell you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll try to recap, in view of the fact that I have already testified about this on a number of occasions, so I will try to relay as -- to the best of my abilities the words that he said to me. He said, You will go to the Bratunac Brigade area of responsibility, you will take over command of the units that are now blocking and searching the terrain, and you will speed up that whole thing. Everything has been organised. The Bratunac Brigade -- or, rather, Colonel Blagojevic has organised it. It is under way, but it is going on -- it's too slow, and we have to speed it up and complete the whole thing in a day or two. A written order will be prepared by General Miletic and forwarded to all units. General Miletic was present. He heard everything that was being said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Anyone else present besides you, General Mladic, and General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether he was there from the outset, but General Tolimir appeared there at some point. Also present there were the then-Colonel Sladojevic, who had joined the VRS a few days ago, and the then-Colonel-later-General Ljubo Obradovic. I don't remember if anyone else was present. It's a huge area with several entrances, but these are the people I remember being present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear at that point that Colonel Sladojevic had a -- also had a job from Mladic on that date?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I did hear Sladojevic and also Trkulja, both of them colonels, and another one, Stankovic. I heard Mladic say that Sladojevic, Trkulja and Stankovic will go to the Zvornik Brigade, assess the situation, and see if they need any assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did he give them that assignment, in relation to your assignment, to go to the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I believe it all happened within a few minutes. He addressed me directly. Now I'm not sure whether he directly addressed Sladojevic or did he actually ask Miletic to put the three of them within the same written order. But it all transpired within a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when is it you recall seeing General Tolimir arrive in this -- in the -- in the bunker?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I remember that General Tolimir was in there, in the ops room. Now was he there already upon my arrival or did he join us later, I can't remember that. But he was present there at some period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell if he was there before, during, or after Mladic gave you the order to go to the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I know it was after; that I know for sure. I don't know whether he was present during or before, but I'm sure that he was there after, because I turned to him and asked him to assist me in clearing up the new situation, and I also wanted to him to assist me in avoiding this impossible task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, first of all, what do you mean "clearing up the new situation"? I'll ask you about the impossible task next.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation was impossible because an officer appears and then immediately he is issued a task that is so serious, so demanding, that it would require a serious command, a Joint Command even, in any army and not for a single lieutenant-colonel. That made the situation impossible, and in any explanation that I tried to give to the commander of the Main Staff was simply ignored by the commander. He just told me what he wanted to tell me, he told General Miletic what he wanted to tell him and left the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when did you contact General Tolimir in regards to General -- the order General Mladic had given to you? Was it before or after Mladic left the room?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, this was all within very short period of time. The whole conversation between myself and the commander of the Main Staff and -- that General Tolimir was actually present when we had our conversation, but I'm not sure about that anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, when you spoke to General Tolimir, was General Mladic present?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I think I've already recounted that one part of the conversation did take place in such a way, but the other part, where we finally reached certain views or decisions, I think then General Mladic was already absent, so I don't think he was present when General Tolimir told me that he will have a word with General Mladic and see if he can change the situation. By that time, Mladic had already left the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you seek Tolimir's assistance in avoiding or changing the order that General Mladic had given you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I sought General Tolimir's assistance, since he was my second commanding officer in the hierarchy. My first commanding officer was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: So I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, could you just remind us who that -- who your first commanding officer was who wasn't present?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: My first commanding officer was Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, go ahead and finish your answer then.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I was not an officer, a commander, who would pick and choose his tasks, but I was also not one of the officers who would carry out any order received. I asked General Tolimir, and I believe I received his support, I asked General Tolimir to help me get an assignment that can be achieved instead of something that was impossible to achieve, no matter how one tried.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you do your best to tell us what you would -- what you mentioned, what you said to General Tolimir? Because this order, on its face, doesn't sound impossible. So what was it that you told General Tolimir about this order and what ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I told both General Tolimir and, prior to that said the same or similar thing to General Mladic, that it's not acceptable and that it's not right to have me take over command of a group of brigades, although I'm not a commander in any of these brigades. I'm an individual there then. I don't have a command. I don't have a staff. I don't have a command post. I have nothing. I don't know the zone or area of responsibility. I would have to get familiarized with it. The group of brigade [as interpreted] already had two colonels serving in them. There was no justification for takeover of command of one such group of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... who were the those two colonels that were already in the group, in your view?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Blagojevic, who was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade; and the commander of the communications regiment, Colonel Gredo. Think his first name was Dusan. He was the commanding officer of the communications regiment, a units that was under blockade. And the Chief of Staff of the special brigades of the Ministry of Interior who was of a rank equivalent to a colonel, his units were there to carry out active operations or to call it more directly, search of terrain. They were --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Excuse me. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: -- commanders of brigade, all of them colonels present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I heard you give the name, I believe, of the special brigade of the Minister of Interior, the MUP. Can you tell us the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Ljubisa Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as best as can you recall, can you tell us what other units General Mladic told you to go and take over. You got the Borovcanin special MUP. You've got -- you've mentioned the communications regiment. Can you tell us the number of that so we get the specific name of that for the record.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I think we had the Bratunac Brigade there; the Milici Brigade, the Light Infantry Brigade from Milici; the MUP forces, I will not specify which unit, I cannot; then some of the forces that were part of the communications regiment; and some of the military policemen from the battalion of the military police of the 65th Protection Regiment. I think those were the units present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember the number of the communications battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Communications regiment, hmm, it had designation 70th and somewhere else it was the 65th. I'm not sure what its number was, because there were seven such regiments in the former Yugoslavia, so it may have received a new designation as 70th, or maybe 65th. But that was the only communications regiment under the Main Staff of the VRS. So the best way of describing it is the communications regiment of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's time to quit for the night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. We have to adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow in the afternoon, 2.15, in Courtroom III. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 11th day of May, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.02 p.m.,
